extracted.intended_audience: graduate students studying algebraic geometry (Math 216 / foundations course)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and usable criteria for central notions in algebraic geometry (smooth/étale/unramified morphisms; generic smoothness; Kleiman–Bertini; depth, Cohen–Macaulayness, Miracle Flatness, and Serre's R1+S2 criterion for normality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck (Gr-EGA) definition of smooth/unramified/étale
rubrics_metrics.description: [Gr-EGA] defines smooth as morphisms that are formally smooth and locally of finite presentation, and similarly for unramified and étale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that these agree with the chapter's definitions for formally unramified and smooth (references given). It also records that the author's definition of unramified as 'formally unramified plus locally of finite type' disagrees with Gr-EGA (see §21.6). Étale is characterized as smooth of relative dimension 0. Suggestion: one may equivalently replace 'nilpotent' by 'square-zero' in the formal lifting test for these formal properties; sometimes the square-zero formulation is easier to work with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness via flatness and regular geometric fibres
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization: smooth morphisms can be described as locally finitely presented, flat, and with regular geometric fibres (see Theorem 25.2.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an alternate, commonly used starting point for defining/recognizing smoothness; the chapter notes that multiple definitions exist and relating them is nontrivial. Use this criterion when checking smoothness via fibre geometry and flatness, especially in geometric applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotangent-complex (naive) characterization of smooth/étale
rubrics_metrics.description: Another characterization of smoothness/étaleness is via (a naive version of) the cotangent complex; this is the approach taken by Stacks (tag 00T2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'less frightening than it sounds' — useful when working with deformation-theoretic or derived techniques. This offers an alternate route to the formal and flatness/regular-fibre definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic smoothness on the source (Theorem 25.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, and let π: X → Y be a dominant morphism of integral k-varieties. Then there is a nonempty (= dense) open set U ⊂ X such that π|_U is smooth of dimension dim X − dim Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key hypotheses: char k = 0 and dominance. Proof uses rank of Ω_{X/Y} at the generic point, upper semicontinuity of fibre rank, generic flatness, and reducedness implies local freeness. Beware: the statement can fail in positive characteristic; Example 25.3.2 exhibits purely inseparable pathologies (e.g., F_p(t)/F_p(t^p)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic smoothness in the target (Theorem 25.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X → Y is a morphism of k-varieties with char k = 0, and X is smooth over k. Then there is a dense open subset U of Y such that π|_{π^{-1}(U)} is a smooth morphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note π^{-1}(U) may be empty if π is not dominant. The proof reduces to Y smooth using generic smoothness on the source and a rank locus dimension bound (Lemma 25.3.4). Again char 0 is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank-locus dimension bound (Lemma 25.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π: X → Y finite type over k, define X_r = { p ∈ X : rank π^*Ω_{Y/k} → Ω_{X/k} at p ≤ r }. Then dim π(X_r) ≤ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets rank(Ω_π|_p) as rank of the tangent map. The lemma is used to bound the dimension of 'bad loci' where the tangent map has small rank; it is a key technical step in proving generic smoothness in the target and Kleiman–Bertini. Exercise 25.3.A asks to check π(X_r) is constructible so its dimension makes sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman–Bertini Theorem (25.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is a homogeneous space for a group variety G over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0. Given morphisms α: Y → X and β: Z → X from smooth k-varieties Y and Z, there is a nonempty open subset V ⊂ G such that for every σ ∈ V(k) the translated intersection Y ×_X (σ·α) Z is smooth of dimension dim Y + dim Z − dim X. Moreover, there is a nonempty open subset of V such that the family over V is a smooth morphism of the indicated relative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in the special case where Y and Z are smooth subvarieties (locally closed embeddings): a general translate of one meets the other transversely. Proof uses generic smoothness on the target twice and equivariance of the action; transitivity of the action upgrades openness to everywhere. Hypotheses: homogeneous space, char 0 (k = k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved characteristic 0 Bertini (Exercise 25.3.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z is a smooth k-variety with char k = 0 and k algebraically closed, and V is a finite-dimensional base-point-free linear series on Z (sections of an invertible sheaf L), then a general element of V (as a closed subscheme of Z) is regular (smooth over k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strengthens classical Bertini in char 0: L need not be very ample nor X projective. Hint: relate to Kleiman–Bertini by taking G = GL(V) and the universal hyperplane. Again fails in positive characteristic (example indicated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of depth (26.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m) and a finitely generated A-module M, depth M is the length of the longest M-regular sequence with elements in m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also mentions I-depth for an ideal I ⊂ R. Exercises give basic properties: depth M = 0 iff every element of m is a zerodivisor on M iff m is an associated prime of M (Exercise 26.1.A). Depth is bounded above by dim Supp M (Exercise 26.1.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomological criterion for regular sequences / depth (Theorem 26.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m) and finitely generated M, the following are equivalent: (i) For every finitely generated A-module N with Supp N = {m}, Ext^i_A(N,M)=0 for all i<n. (ii) Ext^i_A(A/m,M)=0 for all i<n. (iii) There exists an M-regular sequence in m of length n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central cohomological characterization of depth, used to prove uniqueness length of maximal regular sequences (Theorem 26.1.2) and to give vanishing bounds like Lemma 26.1.7. The proof uses long exact sequences in Ext and inductive arguments; it also yields practical computational tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to compute depth by successive non-zerodivisors (26.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute depth M: ask whether there is a zerodivisor x ∈ m on M. (a) If yes, then depth M = 0. (b) If no, choose a non-zerodivisor x ∈ m and replace M by M/xM and repeat; depth drops by 1 each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process terminates by the bound depth M ≤ dim Supp M. Exercise 26.1.E records that depth(M/xM) = depth M − 1 when x is a non-zerodivisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth bounded by dimensions of associated primes (Theorem 26.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth of a module M is at most the smallest dim A/p as p runs over the associated primes of M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strengthens the trivial bound depth M ≤ dim Supp M. The chapter remarks the bound is not always sharp (example: two planes meeting at a point, Exercise 26.1.G). The proof uses Lemma 26.1.7 (Ext vanishing with a shift) and induction on dimension of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cohen–Macaulayness (26.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian local ring (A,m) is Cohen–Macaulay (CM) if depth A = dim A. A locally Noetherian scheme is Cohen–Macaulay if all its local rings are Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises note: schemes of dimension 0 are CM; dimension 1 schemes are CM iff they have no embedded points. Alternate inductive definition via slicing (26.2.8) is given: if dim A > 0 and there exists a non-zerodivisor x ∈ m, then A is CM iff A/(x) is CM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slicing criterion for Cohen–Macaulayness (Theorem 26.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is Noetherian local and x ∈ m is a non-zerodivisor, then (A,m) is Cohen–Macaulay iff (A/x, m) is Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to slicing criteria for regularity and flatness. Geometric interpretation: for an effective Cartier divisor D ⊂ X, if X is CM then D is CM; if D is CM then X is CM at points of D. Useful for inductive proofs and for verifying CM via hyperplane slices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are Cohen–Macaulay (26.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular local rings are Cohen–Macaulay (by Exercise 26.1.F); in particular, smooth schemes over a field are Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields consequences like: effective Cartier divisors on smooth varieties have no embedded points. Also used to deduce regular embeddings in smooth schemes are CM (Proposition 26.2.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embeddings in smooth schemes are Cohen–Macaulay (Proposition 26.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular embeddings in smooth k-schemes are Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence such embeddings have no embedded points; this generalizes hypersurface statements and is leveraged elsewhere (e.g., Exercise 25.2.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle Flatness (algebraic version) (Theorem 26.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose φ: (B,n) → (A,m) is a local homomorphism of Noetherian local rings with A Cohen–Macaulay and B regular, and the fiber A ⊗_B (B/n) has dimension dim A − dim B. Then φ is flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by induction on dim B using choice of non-zerodivisor x ∈ n and the local slicing criterion for flatness. This theorem gives a powerful, very checkable criterion for flatness in the presence of CM and regular hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle Flatness (geometric version) (Theorem 26.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let π: X → Y be a morphism of equidimensional finite type k-schemes with X Cohen–Macaulay, Y regular, and fibers of π have dimension dim X − dim Y. Then π is flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric counterpart of the algebraic Miracle Flatness; applicable to maps between varieties/schemes of finite type. Exercise 26.2.G records that any two of (i) π flat of the stated relative dimension, (ii) X CM, (iii) every fiber X_y is CM of the correct dimension, imply the third (with minor refinements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's R_k and S_k properties (Definition 26.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: R_k: A is regular in codimension k if for every prime p with codim p ≤ k, A_p is regular. S_k: for every prime p of A, depth A_p ≥ min(k, dim A_p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: S_k says local rings are Cohen–Macaulay up to codimension k and have depth at least k beyond that. Notes: S_0 always holds; S_1 ⇔ no embedded points; R_0 + S_1 ⇔ reduced. These properties are standard local conditions used to state Serre's normality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's criterion for normality (Theorem 26.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian ring A is normal iff it has properties R1 and S2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus failure of normality arises from either failure of R1 (singularities in codimension 1) or failure of S2 (a more subtle depth condition). Examples: two planes meeting at a point satisfy R1 but not S2, hence are not normal. The proof is developed in the chapter with integral-domain and general cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: S1 and reducedness equivalences (Exercises 26.3.A–B)
rubrics_metrics.description: S1 ⇔ Spec A has no embedded points. Also, A is reduced (no nilpotents) iff it has R0 and S1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary equivalences help decompose normality criteria and give easy checks for reducedness and embedded points. Useful in examples checking S2 failure vs R1 failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integrally closed (26.3.5 — consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular local rings are integrally closed (integral domains and regular in codimension ≤1 etc. — deduced via Serre's criterion and known facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an alternate route to integrally-closed property for regular local rings without invoking UFD statements; uses that regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay and regular in codimension 1.
